Medicine-05.question: ১) Which one is the most common form of arthritis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is osteoarthritis (OA). It is the most common form of arthritis worldwide, caused by progressive degeneration of articular cartilage with secondary changes in bone.

Features:

  • Degenerative joint disease

  • Commonly affects knees, hips, spine, and hands

  • Associated with age, obesity, and joint stress

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Reactive arthritis → An inflammatory arthritis occurring after infections; less common.

  • Rheumatoid arthritis → A common autoimmune inflammatory arthritis, but not the most common overall.

  • Viral arthritis → Usually acute and self-limiting; uncommon compared with OA.

High-yield points:

Most common arthritis = Osteoarthritis

OA vs RA:

  • OA → Degenerative, cartilage loss, older age

  • RA → Autoimmune, inflammatory, younger/middle age

Exam pearl:
Osteoarthritis is the commonest type of arthritis.

Medicine-05.question: ২) Gout is caused by deposition of which crystals in and around synovial joints?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is monosodium urate monohydrate crystals. Gout occurs due to deposition of urate crystals in and around synovial joints due to hyperuricaemia.

Typical features:

  • Acute inflammatory arthritis

  • Classically affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra)

  • Crystals are needle-shaped and negatively birefringent under polarized light

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Basic calcium phosphate → Associated with calcific periarthritis and some degenerative joint diseases.

  • Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) → Causes pseudogout, commonly affecting the knee.

  • Calcium oxalate → Can cause crystal deposition in patients with severe renal failure or oxalosis.

High-yield points:

Condition Crystal
Gout Monosodium urate monohydrate
Pseudogout Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate
Basic calcium phosphate deposition Calcific tendinitis

Exam pearl:
Gout = Monosodium urate crystals = negatively birefringent.

Medicine-05.question: ৩) Which anti-TB drug causes Gout?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Pyrazinamide. It can cause hyperuricaemia by reducing renal excretion of uric acid, leading to gouty arthritis in susceptible patients.

Mechanism:

  • Pyrazinoic acid (active metabolite of pyrazinamide) inhibits renal tubular secretion of uric acid

  • ↓ Uric acid excretion → ↑ Serum urate → Gout

The other options are incorrect because:

  • INH → Causes peripheral neuropathy, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome.

  • Rifampicin → Causes hepatotoxicity, orange discoloration of body fluids, flu-like syndrome.

  • Ethambutol → Causes optic neuritis and red-green colour blindness.

High-yield anti-TB adverse effects:

Drug Important adverse effect
Pyrazinamide Hyperuricaemia → Gout
Rifampicin Orange body fluids, hepatitis
INH Peripheral neuropathy
Ethambutol Optic neuritis
Streptomycin Ototoxicity

Exam pearl:
Pyrazinamide → Hyperuricaemia → Gout.

Medicine-05.question: ৪) X-ray finding of Osteoarthritis includes-
৫) Example of acute monoarthritis?
৬) Which of the following is a feature of mechanical low back pain?
৭) Which one of the following is multinucleated cells of haematopoietic origin?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is osteoclasts. Osteoclasts are large multinucleated cells of haematopoietic origin derived from the monocyte–macrophage lineage.

Functions:

  • Responsible for bone resorption

  • Secrete acids and enzymes to dissolve bone matrix

  • Located in Howship’s lacunae

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Osteoblasts → Bone-forming cells derived from mesenchymal stem cells; mononuclear.

  • Osteocytes → Mature bone cells derived from osteoblasts; maintain bone matrix.

  • Bone marrow stromal cells → Mesenchymal origin; provide support for haematopoiesis.

High-yield points:

Cell Origin Function
Osteoclast Haematopoietic (monocyte lineage) Bone resorption
Osteoblast Mesenchymal Bone formation
Osteocyte Osteoblast Bone maintenance

Exam pearl:
Multinucleated haematopoietic bone cell = Osteoclast.

Medicine-05.question: ৮) Which of the following hormone Inhibits bone formation?
৯) Which is not a typical feature of Cauda equina syndrome?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is gait disturbance because it is not a typical feature of cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome mainly affects sacral nerve roots (L2–S5) and presents with bladder, bowel, sensory, and lower motor neuron symptoms.

Typical features:

  • Difficulty with micturition (urinary retention)

  • Urinary incontinence (late feature)

  • Saddle anaesthesia (loss of sensation in perineal area)

  • Bilateral leg pain/weakness may occur

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Difficulty with micturition → A classic early warning sign.

  • Urinary incontinence → Severe/late cauda equina involvement.

  • Saddle anaesthesia → Cardinal sensory feature due to S2–S4 root involvement.

High-yield points:

Cauda equina syndrome (red flags):

  • Bladder dysfunction

  • Bowel dysfunction

  • Saddle anaesthesia

  • Sexual dysfunction

  • Lower motor neuron weakness

Exam pearl:
Gait disturbance is not a cardinal feature; bladder dysfunction + saddle anaesthesia are key signs.

Medicine-05.question: ১০) Which one is the analgesic of first choice for mild to moderate pain?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Paracetamol. It is the first-choice analgesic for mild to moderate pain due to its good efficacy and favourable safety profile when used within recommended doses.

Uses:

  • Mild to moderate pain

  • Fever

  • Headache

  • Musculoskeletal pain

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ibuprofen → NSAID used for pain with an inflammatory component; has risks of gastric irritation, renal impairment, and cardiovascular effects.

  • Naproxen → NSAID commonly used for inflammatory pain and arthritis.

  • Indometacin → Potent NSAID used mainly in specific conditions (e.g., acute gout, patent ductus arteriosus), but more adverse effects.

High-yield points:

Analgesic ladder (WHO):

  • Mild pain → Paracetamol ± NSAID

  • Moderate pain → Weak opioid ± non-opioid

  • Severe pain → Strong opioid

Exam pearl:
First-choice analgesic for mild to moderate pain = Paracetamol.

Medicine-05.question: ১১) Which one is the highly specific investigation for diagnosis Rheumatoid arthritis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is ACPA (anti-citrullinated protein antibody). ACPA is a highly specific serological marker for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and can be detected even in early disease.

Key points:

  • ACPA (anti-CCP antibody) → Sensitivity ~60–70%, specificity ~90–95%

  • Predicts more severe, erosive RA

The other options are incorrect because:

  • ANA → Associated mainly with systemic lupus erythematosus and other autoimmune diseases; not specific for RA.

  • ANCA → Used mainly for diagnosis of vasculitis (e.g., granulomatosis with polyangiitis).

  • ESR → A nonspecific marker of inflammation; may be elevated in many conditions.

Exam pearl:
Most specific investigation for rheumatoid arthritis = ACPA (anti-CCP antibody).

Medicine-05.question: ১২) Which one is the most common extra-articular feature of ankylosing spondylitis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is anterior uveitis. It is the most common extra-articular manifestation of ankylosing spondylitis (AS).

Features:

  • Acute anterior uveitis (iritis)

  • Usually unilateral

  • Painful red eye with photophobia and blurred vision

  • Strongly associated with HLA-B27 positivity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fatigue → Can occur due to chronic inflammation but is not the most common specific extra-articular feature.

  • Anaemia → May occur in chronic inflammatory conditions but is not typical of AS.

  • Prostatitis → Not a recognized common extra-articular manifestation.

High-yield points:

Ankylosing spondylitis extra-articular features:

  • Anterior uveitis (most common)

  • Aortic regurgitation

  • Apical pulmonary fibrosis

  • Inflammatory bowel disease

  • Psoriasis

Exam pearl:
Most common extra-articular feature of AS = Acute anterior uveitis.

Medicine-05.question: ১৩) ‘Malar rash’ is a Characteristic feature of-
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). A malar rash (butterfly rash) is a characteristic cutaneous feature of SLE.

Features:

  • Erythematous rash over the cheeks and bridge of the nose

  • Typically spares the nasolabial folds

  • May be triggered or worsened by sunlight (photosensitivity)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) → Characterized by symmetrical inflammatory polyarthritis; may have rheumatoid nodules.

  • Ankylosing spondylitis → Associated with inflammatory back pain, sacroiliitis, and anterior uveitis.

  • Reactive arthritis → Associated with arthritis following infection, conjunctivitis/uveitis, and urethritis.

High-yield points:

SLE features:

  • Malar rash

  • Photosensitivity

  • Oral ulcers

  • Arthritis

  • Serositis

  • Renal involvement

  • Anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm antibodies

Exam pearl:
Malar (butterfly) rash = SLE.

Medicine-05.question: ১৪) Which one of the following is 3rd Cranial nerve?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Oculomotor nerve (CN III). The third cranial nerve is the oculomotor nerve, which supplies most of the extraocular muscles and carries parasympathetic fibres to the eye.

Functions of CN III:

  • Motor supply to:

    • Superior rectus

    • Inferior rectus

    • Medial rectus

    • Inferior oblique

    • Levator palpebrae superioris

  • Parasympathetic supply:

    • Pupil constriction

    • Accommodation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Optic nerve (CN II) → Vision.

  • Trigeminal nerve (CN V) → Facial sensation and muscles of mastication.

  • Vagus nerve (CN X) → Parasympathetic supply to thoracic and abdominal organs; controls swallowing and voice.

High-yield cranial nerve sequence:

I – Olfactory
II – Optic
III – Oculomotor
IV – Trochlear
V – Trigeminal
VI – Abducens

Exam pearl:
3rd cranial nerve = Oculomotor nerve.

Medicine-05.question: ১৫) Root value for ankle jerk is-
১৬) Which cells line the cerebral ventricles?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is ependymal cells. The cerebral ventricles are lined by ependymal cells, which are specialized glial cells derived from neuroepithelium.

Functions of ependymal cells:

  • Line the ventricles and central canal of spinal cord

  • Help in production and circulation of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)

  • Ciliated ependymal cells assist CSF movement

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oligodendrocytes → Produce myelin in the central nervous system.

  • Schwann cells → Produce myelin in the peripheral nervous system.

  • Astrocytes → Maintain blood–brain barrier and provide metabolic support to neurons.

High-yield points:

Neuroglial cells:

  • Ependymal cells → Line ventricles + CSF circulation

  • Astrocytes → BBB support

  • Oligodendrocytes → CNS myelin

  • Microglia → Phagocytosis

  • Schwann cells → PNS myelin

Exam pearl:
Cerebral ventricles are lined by ependymal cells.

Medicine-05.question: ১৭) ‘Auditory perception’ is the function of which lobe of cerebral hemispheres?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is temporal lobe. The primary auditory cortex is located in the superior temporal gyrus (Brodmann areas 41 and 42) and is responsible for auditory perception.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Frontal lobe → Motor function, personality, planning, speech production (Broca’s area).

  • Parietal lobe → Sensory perception, spatial orientation, calculation.

  • Occipital lobe → Visual perception.

High-yield cerebral lobe functions:

Lobe Main function
Frontal Motor, personality, Broca speech
Parietal Sensory, spatial awareness
Temporal Auditory perception, memory
Occipital Vision

Exam pearl:
Auditory perception = Temporal lobe (primary auditory cortex).

Medicine-05.question: ১৮) Which investigation is first line for stroke diagnosis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is CT (non-contrast CT brain). It is the first-line investigation in suspected acute stroke because it rapidly differentiates:

  • Ischaemic stroke (may appear normal early)

  • Intracranial haemorrhage (seen immediately)

This distinction is essential before starting thrombolytic therapy.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • X-rays → Not useful for stroke diagnosis.

  • MRI → More sensitive, especially for early ischaemic stroke, but less available and usually not the first emergency investigation.

  • Duplex scans → Assess carotid artery disease but are not the initial diagnostic test.

High-yield stroke investigations:

  1. Non-contrast CT brain → First-line

  2. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging → Most sensitive for acute ischaemia

  3. Carotid Doppler → Vascular assessment

  4. ECG/Echocardiography → Search for embolic source

Exam pearl:
Acute stroke diagnosis = Non-contrast CT brain first.

Medicine-05.question: ১৯) In which space a needle is inserted for lumber puncture?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is between L4 and L5. A lumbar puncture (LP) is performed in the lower lumbar region to avoid injury to the spinal cord.

Key points:

  • Spinal cord ends at L1–L2 level (conus medullaris)

  • Subarachnoid space extends down to S2

  • CSF is obtained from the lumbar cistern

Common sites for LP:

  • L3–L4

  • L4–L5 (most commonly used)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Between L2 and L3 → May be close to the lower end of the spinal cord; less preferred.

  • Between L5 and S1 → Possible but technically more difficult.

High-yield points:

Lumbar puncture:

  • Site → L3–L4 or L4–L5

  • Patient position → Lateral decubitus or sitting

  • Target → Subarachnoid space containing CSF

Exam pearl:
Most common LP site = L4–L5 interspace.

Medicine-05.question: ২০) High neutrophil count in CSF is diagnostic for which of the following?
২১) Which one is the Upper motor neuron lesion sign?
২২) First-line treatment for focal onset seizure?
২৩) Which one is the most common cause of meningitis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is viruses. Viral meningitis is the most common cause of meningitis overall and is usually less severe than bacterial meningitis.

Common viral causes:

  • Enteroviruses (most common)

  • HSV-2

  • Varicella-zoster virus

  • Mumps virus

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bacteria → Cause acute bacterial meningitis, which is more severe and life-threatening but less common overall.

  • Fungus → Usually occurs in immunocompromised patients (e.g., Cryptococcus).

  • Protozoa → Rare causes of meningitis (e.g., Naegleria fowleri).

High-yield points:

Type CSF predominant cell
Viral meningitis Lymphocytes
Bacterial meningitis Neutrophils
TB meningitis Lymphocytes
Fungal meningitis Lymphocytes

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of meningitis = Viruses.

Medicine-05.question: ২৪) Which organism causes neonatal meningitis?
২৫) Presenting feature of meningitis includes..
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is All above. The classic presenting features of meningitis are:

  • Headache

  • Fever

  • Neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity)

These three features form the classic meningeal irritation triad, although not all patients present with all three.

The other options are incorrect because they represent individual features only.

High-yield points:

Meningitis features:

  • Fever

  • Headache

  • Neck stiffness

  • Photophobia

  • Nausea/vomiting

  • Altered consciousness

  • Seizures (especially severe cases)

Exam pearl:
Meningitis = Fever + Headache + Neck stiffness.

Medicine-05.question: ২৬) Investigation of choice for meningitis?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is CSF study. Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is the investigation of choice for diagnosis of meningitis.

CSF findings help differentiate types of meningitis:

  • Bacterial meningitis

    • ↑ Neutrophils

    • ↑ Protein

    • ↓ Glucose

  • Viral meningitis

    • ↑ Lymphocytes

    • Normal glucose

  • Tuberculous meningitis

    • ↑ Lymphocytes

    • ↑ Protein

    • ↓ Glucose

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CBC → May show leukocytosis but is nonspecific.

  • CT → Done before lumbar puncture in selected patients with risk of raised intracranial pressure, not the diagnostic test of choice.

  • MRI → Useful for complications but not the primary diagnostic investigation.

High-yield points:

Meningitis diagnosis:

  1. CSF analysis by lumbar puncture = investigation of choice

  2. Blood culture → supportive investigation

  3. CT brain → before LP if raised ICP is suspected

Exam pearl:
Investigation of choice for meningitis = CSF study

Medicine-05.question: ২৭) Herpes simplex virus probably reaches the brain via which of the following nerve?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is trigeminal nerve (CN V). Herpes simplex virus (HSV) commonly reaches the brain through retrograde axonal transport along the trigeminal nerve, particularly the ophthalmic division (V1), and remains latent in the trigeminal ganglion.

This is important in:

  • HSV encephalitis

  • Reactivation of latent HSV infection

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Optic nerve (CN II) → Mainly involved in vision; not a common route for HSV spread.

  • Facial nerve (CN VII) → Associated with facial movement and taste; not the typical route for HSV encephalitis.

  • Olfactory nerve (CN I) → A common route for some infections and neuroinvasive viruses, but HSV encephalitis classically involves the trigeminal pathway.

High-yield points:

HSV encephalitis:

  • Route → Trigeminal nerve (CN V)

  • Site affected → Temporal lobes (classically)

  • CSF → Lymphocytic pleocytosis ± RBCs

Exam pearl:
HSV reaches the brain via trigeminal nerve → causes temporal lobe encephalitis.

Medicine-05.question: ২৮) Which one is the initial test for peripheral neuropahty?
২৯) Carpal tunnel syndrome develops due to compression of which nerve?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Median nerve. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) occurs due to compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel at the wrist.

Features of CTS:

  • Numbness and tingling in:

    • Thumb

    • Index finger

    • Middle finger

    • Radial half of ring finger

  • Worse at night

  • Weakness of thenar muscles in severe cases

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ulnar nerve → Causes symptoms in little finger and ulnar half of ring finger (e.g., Guyon canal syndrome).

  • Radial nerve → Supplies wrist/finger extension and dorsal hand sensation.

  • Common peroneal nerve → Lower limb nerve; injury causes foot drop.

High-yield points:

Carpal tunnel contents:

  • Median nerve

  • 9 flexor tendons

Exam pearl:
Carpal tunnel syndrome = Median nerve compression.

Medicine-05.question: ৩০) Which type of stroke is most common?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is ischaemic stroke. It is the most common type of stroke, accounting for approximately 80–85% of all strokes.

Mechanism:

  • Occlusion of a cerebral artery by:

    • Thrombus

    • Embolus

    • Small vessel disease

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Venous stroke → Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is uncommon.

  • Lacunar stroke → A subtype of ischaemic stroke caused by small vessel occlusion.

  • Haemorrhagic stroke → Due to bleeding into brain tissue or subarachnoid space; less common (~15–20%).

High-yield points:

Types of stroke:

  • Ischaemic stroke → 80–85% (most common)

  • Haemorrhagic stroke → 15–20%

Exam pearl:
Most common stroke = Ischaemic stroke.

Medicine-05.question: ৩১) Which of the following is an Organic mental disorder?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Dementias. Organic mental disorders are those caused by physical or structural abnormalities of the brain or other underlying medical conditions.

Examples:

  • Dementia (e.g., Alzheimer’s disease)

  • Delirium due to medical illness

  • Cognitive impairment due to brain injury

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Schizophrenia → A functional psychotic disorder, not primarily due to identifiable brain structural disease.

  • Depression → A functional mood disorder (although biological factors contribute).

  • Bipolar affective disorder → A functional mood disorder.

High-yield points:

Organic mental disorders:

  • Dementia

  • Delirium

  • Mental disorders due to brain disease/injury

Functional psychiatric disorders:

  • Schizophrenia

  • Depression

  • Bipolar disorder

Exam pearl:
Dementia = Organic mental disorder.

Medicine-05.question: ৩২) ‘Misperceptions of real stimuli’ is termed as
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Illusions. An illusion is a misinterpretation or misperception of a real external stimulus.

Examples:

  • Seeing a rope as a snake

  • Mistaking a shadow for a person

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Delusion → A false fixed belief despite evidence to the contrary (e.g., believing someone is trying to harm you).

  • Hallucinations → Perception of something without any external stimulus (e.g., hearing voices when no one is present).

  • Anhedonia → Loss of ability to experience pleasure.

High-yield psychiatric terms:

Term Meaning
Illusion Misinterpretation of real stimulus
Hallucination Perception without stimulus
Delusion False fixed belief
Anhedonia Loss of pleasure

Exam pearl:
Misperception of a real stimulus = Illusion.

Medicine-05.question: ৩৩) Which one is a feature of depression?
৩৪) Which one is a fature of anxiety disorder?
৩৫) Which of the following is a major risk factor for suicide?
৩৬) Which of the following is an antidepressant drug?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is SSRI (Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor). SSRIs are a major class of antidepressant drugs and are commonly used as first-line treatment for depression.

Examples of SSRIs:

  • Fluoxetine

  • Sertraline

  • Citalopram

  • Escitalopram

  • Paroxetine

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Lithium → Mood stabilizer used mainly for bipolar disorder and prevention of relapse.

  • Valproate → Mood stabilizer and antiepileptic; used in bipolar disorder.

  • Lamotrigine → Mood stabilizer, particularly useful for bipolar depression prevention.

High-yield psychotropic drugs:

Drug class Main use
SSRI Depression
Lithium Bipolar disorder
Valproate Bipolar disorder, epilepsy
Lamotrigine Bipolar depression prevention

Exam pearl:
Antidepressant drug = SSRI.

Medicine-05.question: ৩৭) Which type of hallucination usually occurs in Schizophrenia?
৩৮) Which is not a subtype of mood disorder?
৩৯) Dialated pupil found in which of the following poisoning?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Amphetamines. Amphetamine poisoning causes sympathetic overactivity, leading to:

  • Dilated pupils (mydriasis)

  • Tachycardia

  • Hypertension

  • Agitation

  • Hyperthermia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Opioids → Cause constricted pupils (miosis), respiratory depression, and reduced consciousness.

  • Clonidine → Causes miosis, bradycardia, hypotension, and CNS depression.

  • Organophosphorus compounds → Cause miosis with cholinergic features:

    • Salivation

    • Lacrimation

    • Urination

    • Diarrhoea

    • Bronchorrhoea

Medicine-05.question: ৪০) Hyperthermia occurs in which of the following poisoning?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Salicylates. Salicylate poisoning causes hyperthermia due to increased metabolic activity and uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation.

Features of salicylate toxicity:

  • Hyperthermia

  • Tachypnoea (respiratory alkalosis initially)

  • Tinnitus

  • Vomiting

  • Altered mental status

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CNS depressant drugs → Usually cause hypothermia due to reduced metabolic activity and impaired temperature regulation.

  • Opioids → Cause CNS depression, respiratory depression, and may cause hypothermia.

  • Chlorpromazine → Can impair thermoregulation and more commonly causes hypothermia.

Medicine-05.question: ৪১) Gastric lavage is contraindicated in which of the following poisoning?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is all above. Gastric lavage is contraindicated in corrosive and hydrocarbon poisoning because it may worsen injury or increase the risk of aspiration.

Contraindications:

  • Strong acids → Gastric lavage may cause perforation of damaged mucosa.

  • Alkalis → Can worsen caustic injury and increase risk of oesophageal/gastric perforation.

  • Petroleum distillates → High risk of aspiration pneumonitis during lavage.

Exam pearl:

Never do gastric lavage in corrosive (acid/alkali) or hydrocarbon poisoning.

Medicine-05.question: ৪২) Antidote of Paracetamol poisoning is
৪৩) Which one is the Iron Chelating agent?
৪৪) ECG finding in TCA poisoning is..
৪৫) Which of the following is an anticonvulsants drug?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Carbamazepine. It is an anticonvulsant (antiepileptic) drug commonly used for:

  • Focal (partial) seizures

  • Generalised tonic-clonic seizures

  • Trigeminal neuralgia

  • Bipolar disorder (mood stabilisation)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Isoniazid → Anti-tubercular drug; overdose may cause seizures due to pyridoxine deficiency.

  • Theophylline → Bronchodilator; toxicity can cause seizures.

  • Chloroquine → Antimalarial drug; toxicity can cause cardiac arrhythmias and neurological effects.

High-yield antiepileptic drugs:

Drug Main use
Carbamazepine Focal seizures
Lamotrigine Focal/generalised seizures
Valproate Generalised seizures
Ethosuximide Absence seizures

Exam pearl:
Anticonvulsant drug among the options = Carbamazepine.

Medicine-05.question: ৪৬) Which of the following is the muscarinic features of OPC poisoning?
৪৭) The World Health Organisation (WHO) guideline value for arsenic content in tube well water is
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is 10 μg/L. The WHO guideline value for arsenic in drinking water (including tube well water) is 10 micrograms per litre (µg/L).

Key points:

  • Arsenic contamination of groundwater is a major public health issue, especially in parts of South Asia.

  • Chronic arsenic exposure can cause:

    • Skin lesions (hyperkeratosis, pigmentation)

    • Peripheral neuropathy

    • Cardiovascular disease

    • Cancers (especially skin, lung, bladder)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 10 ng/L → Too low and not the WHO guideline limit.

  • 10 mg/L → Extremely high and toxic.

  • 10 g/L → Impossibly high concentration.

High-yield environmental toxicology:

WHO arsenic limit in drinking water = 10 µg/L (0.01 mg/L)

Exam pearl:
Tube well arsenic guideline value = 10 μg/L.

Medicine-05.question: ৪৮) Which one is a Sign of atropinization?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is dilated pupils (mydriasis). Atropinization refers to the clinical effects of adequate atropine therapy, especially in organophosphorus (OPC) poisoning.

Signs of atropinization:

  • Dilated pupils (mydriasis)

  • Dry skin and mouth

  • Reduced bronchial secretions

  • Increased heart rate

  • Flushed skin

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Diplopia → Not a typical sign of atropinization.

  • Miosis → A feature of organophosphorus poisoning, not atropine effect.

  • Lacrimation → Muscarinic feature of OPC poisoning; atropine reduces lacrimation.

High-yield OPC poisoning:

Adequate atropinization = "Dry + Dilated + Fast"

  • Dry secretions

  • Dilated pupils

  • Tachycardia

Exam pearl:
Sign of atropinization = Dilated pupils (mydriasis).

Medicine-05.question: ৪৯) Whinch one is the specific benzodiazepine antagonist?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is Flumazenil. It is a specific benzodiazepine receptor antagonist used to reverse the effects of benzodiazepines.

Mechanism:

  • Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of GABA-A receptors

  • Reverses sedation caused by benzodiazepines

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Naloxone → Specific antidote for opioid poisoning.

  • Acetylcysteine (NAC) → Antidote for paracetamol poisoning.

  • Atropine → Used in organophosphorus poisoning to block muscarinic effects.

High-yield antidotes:

Poison Antidote
Benzodiazepines Flumazenil
Opioids Naloxone
Paracetamol N-acetylcysteine
Organophosphorus Atropine + pralidoxime

Exam pearl:
Benzodiazepine antagonist = Flumazenil.

Medicine-05.question: ৫০) Sudden, severe, ‘thunderclap’ headache, these are typical features of which of the following?
Medicine-05.exp:
The correct answer is subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). A sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache is the classic presenting feature of SAH, often described as:

  • “Worst headache of my life”

  • Sudden onset reaching maximum intensity within seconds to minutes

  • May be associated with:

    • Neck stiffness

    • Vomiting

    • Loss of consciousness

    • Photophobia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ischaemic stroke → Usually presents with focal neurological deficits (weakness, speech disturbance, visual symptoms); headache is less prominent.

  • Migraine → Can cause severe headache but usually has a gradual onset and may have aura, photophobia, and nausea.

  • Trigeminal neuralgia → Causes brief, electric shock-like facial pain triggered by touch or movement.

High-yield points:

Thunderclap headache causes:

  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage (classic)

  • Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

  • Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome

  • Pituitary apoplexy

Exam pearl:
Sudden “worst headache of life” = Subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise.
